summary: The article looks at how the Internet of Things (IoT) is reshaping supply chain management in small and medium enterprises (SMEs), drawing on interviews with leaders at several companies. They describe gains in delivery times, quality control, warehousing, data sharing, cost and competitiveness, along with challenges such as limited resources and the need for workforce upskilling. It concludes that IoT is already a present reality for SMEs, not just for large corporations.
one_line: Interviews with SME leaders show how IoT improves supply chain efficiency, transparency, costs and competitiveness, despite resource challenges and skills needs.
key_facts: Susan Clark, operations director at FreshCart Produce, an organic food SME established in September 2023, integrated IoT using IoT-enabled vehicles and smart inventory systems.
FreshCart Produce achieved what Susan Clark calls 'near-perfect' delivery times and drastically reduced food waste; its IoT change began with real-time temperature monitoring during transit.

John Davies, CEO of TechFabrics, a small industrial smart textile manufacturer, said the company lacked in-house expertise and financial muscle, so it partnered with IoT service providers and tech startups to adopt IoT without the usual overhead.
TechFabrics uses IoT sensors to monitor production processes and materials, ensuring quality control and reducing downtime from machinery failure.
Lisa Wong, head of supply chain at EcoLighting Solutions, said IoT lets the company share inventory levels, demand forecasts and sustainability data with partners in real time.
Michael Brown, warehouse manager at Swift Distribution, said the warehouse became a model of efficiency within a year using IoT-enabled smart shelving and autonomous forklifts.
Swift Distribution's system anticipates stock-outs and adjusts orders, reducing overstocking and understocking and improving cash flow management and customer satisfaction.
Alex Green, founder of PureHarvest, which supplies organic ingredients to major food retailers, said smart sensors let the small supplier provide the same level of detail as larger competitors.
Miranda Lee, CFO at QuickFix Hardware, treated IoT as a long-term investment and began seeing cost decreases within six months, which translated into competitive pricing for customers.

Robert Peterson, head of human resources at Craft & Build, a mid-sized construction supplier, said the company committed to upskilling its workforce through regular training sessions and work with technical colleges.
The article concludes that IoT is not an exclusive domain of large corporations and offers benefits in efficiency, cost reduction and competitive edge.
